name: xjb
baseline: Ryu (ulfjack/ryu, the double-to-shortest-string algorithm that std::to_chars uses in libstdc++, libc++ and MSVC STL; std::to_chars itself is not in the benchmark); also benchmarked against Dragonbox, Schubfach and fmt 12.1.0
workload: Converting 16M random IEEE-754 doubles (random bit patterns over the whole binary range, NaN and Inf filtered) to shortest round-trip decimal strings; further datasets cover random digit counts, fixed digit counts, [0,1) doubles, integers, subnormals and floats.
claimed_speedup: Result file for GCC 13.3.0 on AMD Ryzen 7 7840H, random doubles, cycles per conversion: xjb64 60.5, ryu 142.5, dragonbox_full 105.8, dragonbox_comp 116.2, fmt_full 132.2, schubfach 127.7, zmij 93.9, yy_double 89.9, i.e. about 2.4x faster than Ryu, 1.75x faster than Dragonbox, 2.2x faster than fmt (derived from page data). On Apple M1 with Apple clang 17.0.0 the same chart reads xjb64 31.4, ryu 98.7, fmt_full 98.3, dragonbox_comp 100.4, about 3.1x faster than Ryu (derived from page data). 'random length' dataset, GCC 13.3.0: xjb64 62.9 vs ryu 199.4.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (result file); bench/makefile builds with -O3 -std=c++20 -march=native -DNDEBUG for g++, icpx and clang++
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7840H w/ Radeon 780M Graphics, 5115 MHz reported, Linux x86-64 (also Apple M1, Apple clang 17.0.0)
stars_or_usage: 46 stars; used by ssrJSON and jsoniter-scala per README
tradeoffs: Single-file implementation with lookup tables (full: 15336 bytes double, 1352 bytes float; compressed: 368 and 64 bytes). Derived from Schubfach and produces identical digits to Schubfach (make check in bench). Uses SIMD (NEON, AVX512IFMA paths credited to dougallj and lemire). Output format is its own (for example 1000 prints as '1000.0', 0 as '0.0', NaN as 'nan'), with a separate JSON variant, so it is not a drop-in for std::to_chars. Big-endian is not supported yet; f80, f128 not supported.
caveats: First-party benchmark run by the author; no peer review. The README's license line says MIT but the LICENSE file and the src/ftoa.cpp header are Apache-2.0 (the awesome-cpp list also says Apache-2.0), so the license is recorded as Apache-2.0; the bench/ directory vendors third-party code (schubfach, ryu, dragonbox, fmt, yy, zmij, teju, uscale) under its own licenses, which the library sources do not need. std::to_chars is not benchmarked; Ryu stands in for it, and the Ryu entry prints its own exponent format, so output formats differ across rows. Cycles come from rdtsc, so values are TSC ticks and only ratios are meaningful. In the newer result files (GCC 15.2.0, Clang 21.1.6, Clang 17 on M1) the xjb64_comp, yyjson and jnum rows sit at about 8 cycles in every dataset, barely above the 5-cycle null baseline, which looks like optimized-away work; the GCC 13.3.0 file does not show this and was used for the headline numbers. The xjb64 row is the one cited. Results differ by compiler: with Clang 21.1.6 on the same CPU xjb64 is 71.1 vs ryu 132.5 cycles (about 1.9x), and with GCC 15.2.0 55.7 vs 144.4 (about 2.6x) (derived from page data).

name: Yomm2
baseline: C++ virtual member function call (closed dispatch via vtable)
metric: latency (average time per dispatched call, unit not stated on the page)
workload: Google Benchmark loop picking a random hierarchy out of 100, then a random object (or two for arity 2) out of 1000 per hierarchy with randomized allocation sizes, and calling one virtual function or the equivalent open method; ordinary-inheritance and virtual-inheritance variants.
claimed_speedup: Only the virtual_ptr rows beat the baseline. docs/benchmarks/v010500.euclid.clang.md (clang 16.0.6, 100 hierarchies of 1000 objects), arity 1 ordinary base: virtual function 60.1, direct virtual ptr 10.5 (ratio 0.18), indirect virtual ptr 12.2 (0.20); arity 2: virtual function 93.2, direct virtual ptr 19.4 (0.21), indirect 20.5 (0.22), i.e. about 5x lower time per call (derived from page data). With virtual inheritance the same rows are 2.1x slower than the virtual function (arity 1: 74.3 vs 156.9). The README states the headline opposite: dispatch with one virtual argument takes 15-30% more time than the equivalent virtual member function.
compiler_and_flags: clang 16.0.6, build type release (CMake Release; exact flags not stated in the result file)
hardware: host 'euclid', '16 X 3300 MHZ CPUs' (CPU model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 382 stars; packaged in Conan Center and vcpkg
tradeoffs: Open (non-intrusive) multi-methods for C++17 with multiple dispatch on several arguments, which virtual functions cannot do; needs class registration and a runtime update() call that builds dispatch tables (about 75K runtime). Plain-reference dispatch costs 9 instructions and 7 memory reads vs 2 and 2 for a virtual call; virtual_ptr is a fat pointer (extra pointer size) that carries the vptr. Dispatch through virtual bases needs a dynamic cast and is 2-5x slower than virtual functions.
caveats: Weak evidence of 'faster'. The repo is archived (2026-03-04) and superseded by Boost.OpenMethod (Boost 1.90); the README now says YOMM2 'was' a library. The author's own text says open methods are almost as fast as virtual functions and 15-30% slower with plain references, and docs/benchmarks show ratios of 1.06-1.62 for the non-virtual_ptr rows (for example arity 1 ordinary base: basic policy 80.4 vs virtual function 60.1). The 0.18-0.22 ratios for virtual_ptr come from a layout effect in the benchmark: the virtual_ptr rows read the vptr from a contiguous vector of fat pointers, while the virtual function row dereferences each randomly chosen heap object, so object cache misses dominate the baseline (tests/benchmarks.cpp, population::draw vs vptr_draw). The result file gives no time unit and no CPU model, and the benchmark source disables g++ ('Don't benchmark g++ until this is fixed'). The 'much faster than other implementations' claim in docs/articles/performance.md has no numbers. First-party measurement, so tier C.
